1. Clinical Guidance

  • Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)

2. Definitions

  • Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB): Uterine bleeding that is abnormal in frequency, duration, regularity, or volume in a nonpregnant individual of reproductive age.
  • AUB patterns:
  • Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB): Excessive bleeding that interferes with quality of life or results in anemia.
  • Intermenstrual Bleeding (IMP): Bleeding between otherwise regular menstrual cycles.
  • Prolonged Menstrual Bleeding: Bleeding lasting >7 days in a single cycle.
  • Irregular Bleeding: Inconsistent cycle length (>20 days variation cycle to cycle).
  • Frequent Menstruation: Menstrual bleeding occurring more often than every 21 days.
  • Infrequent Menstruation: Bleeding occurring at intervals >35 days but <6 months (oligomenorrhea).
  • Spotting: Minimal bleeding that does not fulfill criteria for IMB or HMB.
  • Postcoital Bleeding (PCB): Bleeding following sexual intercourse; may coexist with AUB but also suggests lower genital tract pathology.
  • PALM–COEIN categories:
  • Polyp.
  • Adenomyosis.
  • Leiomyoma.
  • Malignancy & Hyperplasia.
  • Coagulopathy.
  • Ovulatory dysfunction.
  • Endomterial origin.
  • Iatrogenic.
  • Not yet classified.

3. Scope

  • This guideline applies to the diagnostic evaluation of patients presenting with:
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding.
  • Intermenstrual bleeding.
  • Irregular or prolonged menstrual bleeding.
  • Frequent or infrequent menstrual cycles.
  • Postcoital bleeding suspected to originate from the uterus.
  • Persistent unexplained uterine bleeding.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • Bleeding during confirmed pregnancy (miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, gestational trophoblastic disease).
  • Purely cervical or vaginal bleeding unrelated to uterine origin.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding pathways.
  • Management/treatment protocols.
  • Obstetric hemorrhage.
  • Known gynecologic malignancy surveillance.

  • Life stage: adolescent / reproductive age / peri- or postmenopause.
  • Bleeding pattern: as per above definitions.
  • PALM–COEIN working category (at least “suspected structural vs non-structural”).

6. Coverage criteria - Laboratory testing

  • In all reproductive-age females pregnancy test is mandatory.
  • Investigations should be directed by the clinical suspecion based on the FIGO-PALM-COEIN categories.
  • Baseline laboratory testing: (Approve at first visit) In patients without a known hemostatic disorder:
  • CBC.
  • Ferritin.
  • Pregnancy test.
  • Conditional tests:
  • TSH (when endocrine or ovulatory dysfunction is suspected).
  • LH, FSH, prolactin (when anovulation, pituitary-ovarian dysfunction, galactorrhea, or endocrine disorder is suspected).
  • Calculated free testosterone, calculated bioavailable testosterone, or free androgen index (If PCOS suspected and labs required for Rotterdam criteria).
  • PT, aPTT, Fibrinogen +/- VWD and hematology consultation (if heavy bleeding + any of the following):
  • Heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche.
  • ≥1 of: postpartum hemorrhage, surgery-related bleeding, bleeding associated with dental work.
  • ≥2 of the following symptoms: bruising 1-2 times/month, epistaxis 1-2 times/month, frequent gum bleeding, family history of bleeding symptoms.

7. Coverage criteria - Imaging

  • 1) TVUS if any of the following:
  • Structural cause suspected.
  • Abnormal pelvic exam.
  • Persistent or recurrent AUB.
  • Suspected fibroid, polyp, adenomyosis, endometrial thickening.
  • 2) Color flow Doppler can be added to TVUS for the following conditions:
  • 1. Distinguishing adenomyosis vs fibroids.
  • 2. Differentiating polyps vs submucosal leiomyoma.
  • 3. Suspected uterine AV malformation.
  • 3) Saline infusion sonography (SIS) can be added to TVUS for the following conditions:
  • 1. Intracavitary lesion suspected.
  • 2. TVUS nondiagnostic.
  • 3. Need to better define polyp or submucosal myoma.
  • 4) MRI pelvis approved if any of the following:
  • Adenomyosis vs leiomyoma remains unclear.
  • Mapping submucosal myoma extent.
  • Complex anatomy before intervention.
  • *Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is not routine for AUB workup.

8. Coverage criteria - Office-based procedures

  • 1. Age ≥45 years old.
  • 2. Age <45 years old as below:
  • Any abnormal uterine bleeding in patients with BMI ≥30 kg/m2.
  • In patients with BMI <30 kg/m2, abnormal uterine bleeding that is persistent and occurs in the setting of one of the following: chronic ovulatory dysfunction, other exposure to estrogen unopposed by progesterone,
  • failed medical management of the bleeding, or patients at high risk of endometrial cancer (eg, Lynch syndrome, Cowden syndrome).
  • Premenopausal women who are anovulatory and have prolonged periods of amenorrhea (≥6 months).
  • 3. Any of the following pap smear results:
  • o Presence of AGC-endometrial.

  • o Presence of benign-appearing endometrial cells in patients ≥40 years of age who also have abnormal uterine bleeding or risk factors for endometrial cancer.

  • 1. Cervical pathology suspected.

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Severe Asthma – Biologic Therapy

2. Definitions

  • 1. Asthma: A heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough) and variable expiratory airflow limitation.
  • 2. Difficult-to-Treat Asthma: Persistent asthma symptoms and/or exacerbations despite prescribing of medium or high-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) combined with another controller (e.g., LABA), or maintenance oral
  • corticosteroids (OCS), after confirmation of diagnosis, treatment adherence, and comorbidity management.
  • 3. Severe Asthma: Asthma requiring high-dose ICS plus a second controller (e.g., LABA ± LAMA) to prevent it from becoming uncontrolled, ORasthma that remains uncontrolled despite this therapy. Specifically, BOTH of the following
  • must be present:
  • Demonstrated variable airflow limitation (spirometry or bronchoprovocation testing).
  • Frequent or persistent symptoms: cough, wheeze, or dyspnea >2 times/week; activity limitation; nocturnal awakening; AND/OR frequent exacerbations (≥1 hospitalization or ≥2 OCS-requiring exacerbations per year).
  • 4. Type 2 (T2) Airway Inflammation: The predominant inflammatory endotype in severe asthma, driven by Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) and upstream alarmins (TSLP, IL-33). Characterized by eosinophilic inflammation, elevated
  • FeNO, and IgE-mediated allergic sensitization.
  • 5. Blood Eosinophil Count (BEC): A key biomarker for T2 inflammation, measured as cells/µL.
  • 6. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): A non-invasive biomarker of eosinophilic airway inflammation, expressed in parts per billion (ppb).
  • 7. Biologic Therapy (Add-on): Monoclonal antibodies targeting specific molecular pathways involved in T2 airway inflammation, used as add-on therapy at GINA Step 5 for severe uncontrolled asthma.
  • Approved biologic classes:
  • Anti-IgE: Omalizumab (Xolair).
  • Anti-IL-5: Mepolizumab.
  • Anti-IL-5 receptor (IL-5Rα): Benralizumab.
  • Anti-IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα, targeting IL-4 and IL-13): Dupilumab (Dupixent).
  • Anti-TSLP (thymic stromal lymphopoietin): Tezepelumab.

3. Scope

  • This guideline applies to the coverage evaluation of biologic add-on therapy for patients presenting with:
  • Confirmed severe asthma at GINA Step 5 (uncontrolled on high-dose ICS-LABA ± LAMA).
  • Adolescents (≥12 years) and adults, except where a specific biologic is approved from age ≥6.
  • Referral from a specialist (pulmonologist or allergist/immunologist).
  • This guideline does NOTcover:
  • Mild-to-moderate asthma not meeting Step 5 criteria.
  • First-line or step-down controller therapy.
  • Acute exacerbation management.
  • Non-asthma indications for the same biologics (e.g., atopic dermatitis, nasal polyposis).
  • Pediatric patients under age 6.
  • Non-biologic management protocols.

4. Policy

  • Requirements for coverage

5. Documentation requirements

  • Confirmed asthma diagnosis with spirometric evidence of variable airflow limitation.
  • GINA Step 5 treatment failure: documented high-dose ICS-LABA (± LAMA) use for ≥3 months with persistent uncontrolled asthma.
  • Evidence of adherence to current therapy and correct inhaler technique.
  • Documented assessment and optimization of modifiable risk factors and comorbidities (rhinosinusitis, GERD, obesity, OSA, anxiety/depression).
  • Specialist referral (pulmonologist or allergist/immunologist) with documented phenotyping and biomarker assessment.
  • Documented asthma control level (ACQ-6 or ACT score) and exacerbation history in the prior 12 months.

6. Coverage criteria - Pre-Biologic Evaluation

  • The following workup must be completed and documented prior to biologic initiation:
  • 1) Confirm diagnosis and rule out alternatives:
  • Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility (≥12% and 200 mL increase in FEV1, OR bronchoprovocation if pre-BD spirometry is normal).
  • Rule out vocal cord dysfunction, COPD, bronchiectasis, cardiac causes.
  • 2) Baseline laboratory testing:
  • Full blood count with differential (BEC).
  • Total serum IgE.
  • Skin-prick testing (SPT) ORallergen-specific serum IgE (for allergic phenotyping).
  • FeNO measurement (if available).
  • Spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) — current values and historical.
  • 3) Biomarker thresholds for T2 inflammation (GINA 2025):
  • BEC ≥300 cells/µL: typical threshold for T2-targeted biologic eligibility.
  • BEC ≥150 cells/µL: suggests T2 inflammation; may meet threshold in clinical context.
  • FeNO >50 ppb (ICS-naïve); FeNO ≥25 ppb (medium-dose ICS); FeNO ≥20 ppb (high-dose ICS): elevated threshold values.
  • Note: BEC and FeNO should be measured ≥3 times if not initially above target threshold. Oral corticosteroids suppress eosinophils and FeNO — historical values preferred when patient is on OCS.
  • 4) Exacerbation burden (minimum required for coverage):
  • ≥2 severe exacerbations requiring systemic OCS in the past 12 months, OR
  • ≥1 hospitalization for asthma in the past 12 months, OR
  • Maintenance OCS dependence (ongoing use ≥3 months to maintain asthma control).

7. Coverage criteria - Biologic Agent Selection

  • Agent selection is guided by the patient's T2 inflammatory profile, comorbidities, biomarker levels, age, and clinical context. The table below summarizes each agent's key criteria:

8. Coverage criteria - Agent-Specific Eligibility

  • 1) Omalizumab “Xolair” – Anti-IgE:
  • Confirmed sensitization to at least one perennial inhaled allergen (positive SPT ≥3mm or allergen-specific IgE ≥0.35 kU/L).
  • Total serum IgE 30–1500 IU/mL.
  • Body weight and IgE level within the approved dosing table.
  • Note: Omalizumab has no well-established OCS-sparing effect — use with caution in maintenance OCS- dependent patients.
  • 2) Mepolizumab – Anti-IL-5:
  • BEC ≥150 cells/µL while on high-dose ICS, OR ≥300 cells/µL at any point in the prior 12 months.
  • Preferred agent when nasal polyposis is a comorbidity (also approved for CRSwNP).
  • Approved from age ≥6 years.
  • 3) Benralizumab – Anti-IL-5Rα:
  • BEC ≥150 cells/µL while on high-dose ICS, OR ≥300 cells/µL at any point in the prior 12 months.
  • Often preferred for dosing convenience (every 8 weeks after initial loading doses).
  • Approved from age ≥12 years.
  • 4) Dupilumab (Dupixent ) – Anti-IL-4Rα:
  • BEC ≥150 cells/µL OR FeNO ≥20–25 ppb (consistent with T2-high profile).
  • Preferred in OCS-dependent patients (established OCS-sparing efficacy).
  • Preferred when atopic comorbidities coexist (atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic esophagitis — also approved for these indications).
  • Approved from age ≥6 years.
  • 5) Tezepelumab – Anti-TSLP:
  • No mandatory BEC or FeNO threshold required for eligibility.
  • Approved for severe uncontrolled asthma in patients aged ≥12 years, regardless of eosinophilic phenotype.
  • First-line option when BEC <150 cells/µL and no T2 biomarker signal is present (T2-low phenotype).
  • Also shows increased efficacy in T2-high patients (elevated BEC or FeNO).

9. Coverage criteria - Biologic Comorbidity Alignment

  • When a relevant T2 comorbidity exists, coverage should preferentially align with a single biologic agent approved for both asthma and the comorbidity:
  • Comorbidity Preferred Biologic(s) Alternatives Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal Mepolizumab, Dupilumab (Dupixent) Omalizumab “Xolair” (childhood-onset
  • polyposis (CRSwNP) asthma), Tezepelumab (phase III trials) Atopic dermatitis (eczema) Dupilumab — Eosinophilic esophagitis Dupilumab —
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with Mepolizumab, Benralizumab — polyangiitis (EGPA) Allergic bronchopulmonary Omalizumab, Dupilumab Mepolizumab
  • aspergillosis (ABPA) Chronic spontaneous urticaria Omalizumab —

10. Coverage criteria - Treatment Response and Continuation

  • All biologic approvals are conditional on demonstrated clinical response. Reassessment must occur at 4–6 months after initiation. Continuation requires documentation of ≥1 of the following response criteria:
  • ≥50% reduction in annualized exacerbation rate.
  • ≥50% reduction in maintenance OCS dose (OCS-dependent patients).
  • Clinically meaningful improvement in asthma control score (ACQ-6 decrease ≥0.5, or ACT increase ≥3 points).
  • Meaningful improvement in FEV1 or quality of life in clinical judgment.
  • If inadequate response at 4–6 months:
  • Reassess diagnosis, adherence, and comorbidities.
  • Consider switching to an alternative biologic from a different class if patient meets eligibility criteria.
  • Macrolide therapy (low-dose azithromycin) and/or low-dose maintenance OCS are reasonable when no biologic option is available or effective.
  • Biologic discontinuation:
  • A trial of discontinuation should not be considered until after ≥12 months of treatment with well-maintained asthma control.
  • Only consider if asthma remains well-controlled on at least medium-dose ICS-containing therapy.
  • For allergic asthma (omalizumab “Xolair”): ensure no ongoing relevant allergen exposure before discontinuation.

1. Clinical Guidance

  • in Chronic Migraine

2. Definitions

  • Chronic migraine: headache occurring on 15 or more days per month for more than three months, with the features of migraine headache on at least eight of those days.
  • Episodic migraine: headache occurring on fewer than 15 days per month.
  • Preventive (prophylactic) medicine: an agent taken regularly to reduce the frequency and severity of migraine attacks, as distinct from the acute treatment of an individual attack.
  • Treatment cycle: a single administration of onabotulinumtoxinA across the full set of injection sites; cycles are given no more often than every 12 weeks.

3. Scope

  • This guideline covers requests for botulinum toxin type A (onabotulinumtoxinA) given by intramuscular injection for the prevention of chronic migraine in adults, for both the initial course of treatment and for
  • continuation beyond that course.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • Episodic migraine, that is fewer than 15 headache days per month.
  • Tension-type headache, cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia, cervicogenic headache and all other headache disorders.
  • The acute treatment of a migraine attack.
  • Patients under 18 years of age.
  • Botulinum toxin preparations other than onabotulinumtoxinA. Botulinum toxin products are not interchangeable and their potency units cannot be converted between preparations.

4. Policy

  • Botulinum toxin type A is covered for the prevention of chronic migraine only where all of criteria A, B and C are met.
  • A: The patient is aged 18 years or over and has a diagnosis of chronic migraine made by a neurologist, that is headache on 15 or more days per month for more than three months with migraine features on at least eight
  • of those days, recorded on a headache diary.
  • B: At least three preventive medicines have not worked, were not tolerated, or are unsuitable on safety grounds. Each oral agent must have been taken for at least eight weeks at the target dose before being judged
  • to have failed.
  • C: Where acute headache medication is overused, the overuse has been identified and the medication withdrawn before treatment begins.
  • Covered dose and frequency:
  • The covered regimen is onabotulinumtoxinA 155 units, given as 5 units per 0.1 mL at each of 31 injection sites divided bilaterally as set out in Table 1, repeated once every 12 weeks. An initial course of three cycles
  • is covered.
  • Doses above 155 units, injections at more than 31 sites, and repeat injection earlier than 12 weeks after the previous cycle are not covered.
  • Continuation of treatment:
  • A fourth or subsequent cycle is covered only where all of the following are met.
  • Three cycles have been completed, each given at least 12 weeks apart, with a headache diary kept throughout.
  • Headache days per month have fallen by at least 30 per cent compared with the headache diary kept before the first cycle.
  • The condition has not changed to episodic migraine, that is fewer than 15 headache days per month, for three consecutive months.
  • Where these are met, one further cycle is covered, to be given no earlier than 12 weeks after the previous cycle. Treatment is not covered once the condition has been episodic migraine for three consecutive months.

5. Documentation Requirements

  • 1. A neurologist report stating the diagnosis of chronic migraine and the date it was made.
  • 2. The headache diary covering the month before the request, showing headache days and migraine days.
  • 3. The names, doses and durations of the preventive medicines tried, with the reason each was stopped.
  • 4. For a continuation request, the dates of the previous cycles, the units given at each, and the headache diary kept before the first cycle.

1. Definition

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) refers to the complex of symptoms and signs brought on by compression of the median nerve as it travels through the carpal tunnel. Patients commonly experience pain and paresthesia, and less commonly weakness, in the
  • median nerve distribution.
  • CTS categorized based on clinical symptoms into:
  • Mild symptoms: non-persistent numbness or weakness. Symptoms do not disrupt sleep, impair hand function, or interfere with activities of daily living (ADLs).
  • Moderate symptoms: Persistent numbness or mild nocturnal symptoms occasionally disrupt sleep. Symptoms may interfere slightly with hand function, but the patient is able to perform all ADLs.
  • Severe CTS symptoms: Symptoms are disabling, routinely disrupt sleep, or prevent the patient from carrying out one or more ADLs.
  • CTS further categorized based on electrodiagnostic testing into:
  • Mild CTS: prolonged (relative or absolute) sensory latencies; motor studies are normal. There is no evidence for axon loss.
  • Moderate: prolonged sensory and motor latencies. There is no evidence of axon loss.
  • Severe: characterized by evidence of axon loss, as defined by any of the following:
  • o Absent or low-amplitude sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) or mixed nerve action potential
  • o Low-amplitude or absent thenar compound muscle action potential (CMAP)
  • o Needle electromyography (EMG) with fibrillation potentials or motor unit potential changes

2. Scope

  • This guideline outlined the diagnosis, management of carpal tunnel syndrome

3. Policy

  • Eligibility/coverage criteria:
  • o Diagnosis:
  • Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on characteristic symptoms and physical findings.
  • Diagnostic testing is indicated in patients with moderate to severe symptoms or when the diagnosis is uncertain. It may also be considered in patients with mild symptoms who show disease progression despite optimal conservative management.
  • Nerve Conduction Study (NCS): Initial electrodiagnostic test and is recommended for patients with moderate to severe or atypical symptoms.
  • Electromyography (EMG): Reserved for patients with atypical symptoms to exclude alternative diagnoses or when nerve decompression surgery is being considered.
  • Imaging (Ultrasound or MRI): Performed only in patients with atypical presentations where electrodiagnostic studies fail to explain
  • the symptoms. It is useful for identifying anatomical variants or secondary causes of CTS, such as tumors, ganglion cyst, bifid median
  • nerve, or bone abnormalities.
  • o Management:
  • First-line:
  • Wrist splinting ± corticosteroid injection — Recommended for all patients, including those with moderate to severe symptoms, provided there is no evidence of axonal loss.
  • Second-line:
  • Physical therapy (Modalities: Carpal bones Mobilization/Manual therapy, Nerve gliding exercises, or therapeutic ultrasound) Offered
  • to patients who do not respond to 1st line therapy provided there is no axonal loss or worsening of symptoms.
  • Third-line:
  • Nerve decompression surgery — Indicated for patients with evidence of axonal loss, progressive neurological symptoms, or failure of
  • conservative (non-surgical) management.
  • Requirements for Coverage
  • o ICD-10 and SBS codes must be coded to the highest level of specificity
  • Insurance Documentation Requirement:
  • o Initial diagnosis report
  • Comprehensive details on symptoms, signs, diagnostic testing, and severity level
  • o Treatment records
  • Documented prescribed treatment, duration and patient response
  • Non-coverage:
  • o The following treatment has no evidence and shall not be covered:
  • NSAIDs
  • Electrical, magnetic, and laser therapy
  • Perineural dextrose injections Appendix.1

  • Screening can be done via various laboratory tests methods such as Hemoglobin A1C (HgA1C), Fasting blood sugar (FBS), 75 oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), each has its own advantages and disadvantages.

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Dyslipidemia – Advanced Lipid-Lowering Therapy: Biologic & Novel Agent

2. Definitions

  • 1) Dyslipidemia: Abnormal levels of one or more lipid fractions: elevated LDL-C, non-HDL-C, triglycerides (TG), or Lp(a); or reduced HDL-C. Causally associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).
  • 2) ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease): Includes coronary artery disease (CAD/MI), ischemic stroke/TIA, symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD), and other atherosclerotic vascular events.
  • 3) ApoB (Apolipoprotein B): One particle per atherogenic lipoprotein; more strongly associated with ASCVD events than LDL-C when using Friedewald estimation. Useful when LDL-C and apoB are discordant. Target: <65 mg/dL
  • (very high risk), <80 mg/dL (high risk).
  • 4) Lp(a) (Lipoprotein(a)): A genetically determined, causal, independent ASCVD risk factor not captured by standard lipid panels. Universal once-in-a-lifetime screening is a Class I (Level A) recommendation in 2026
  • ACC/AHA. Threshold of clinical significance: ≥125 nmol/L (≥50 mg/dL).
  • 5) Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH):
  • Heterozygous FH (HeFH): Autosomal dominant mutation causing LDL-C typically 160–400 mg/dL. Prevalence ~1:250. Diagnosed by Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) or Simon Broome criteria, or genetic testing.
  • Homozygous FH (HoFH): Biallelic mutations; LDL-C often >400 mg/dL; extremely high ASCVD risk; requires specialized therapies including PCSK9i, evinacumab, and/or lomitapide.
  • 6) PCSK9 Inhibitors (Biologics):
  • Monoclonal antibodies (evolocumab “Repatha”, alirocumab “Praluent”) targeting PCSK9 — a serine protease that degrades LDL receptors. Inhibition upregulates hepatic LDL-R, reducing LDL-C by 50–65% on top of statin
  • therapy.
  • Inclisiran “Leqvio”: A small interfering RNA (siRNA) — not a monoclonal antibody but a biologic-class agent — that silences PCSK9 synthesis in hepatocytes. Twice-yearly SC dosing. Similar LDL-C reduction to mAbs.
  • 7) Evinacumab: The only agent effective in HoFH with absent LDL-R activity.
  • 8) Maximally Tolerated Statin Therapy (MTST): The highest statin dose the patient can tolerate without unacceptable muscle or other adverse effects, including high-intensity statin (rosuvastatin 20–40 mg or atorvastatin
  • 40–80 mg) or moderate-intensity if intolerant. MTST is a prerequisite before most advanced agents.
  • 1

3. Scope

  • This guideline applies to the coverage evaluation of advanced lipid-lowering therapy (PCSK9 inhibitors, inclisiran, evinacumab, bempedoic acid, and other novel agents) for:
  • Adults with clinical ASCVD (secondary prevention) not at LDL-C goal on MTST ± ezetimibe.
  • Adults with familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH or HoFH) not at goal on MTST ± ezetimibe.
  • Adults with severe hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL) without FH criteria, not at goal.
  • Adults with high-risk primary prevention profiles (diabetes, CKD, Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L) not at goal.
  • Adults with confirmed statin intolerance requiring alternative non-statin agents.
  • This guideline does NOTcover:
  • Mild or moderate dyslipidemia manageable with lifestyle + standard statin therapy.
  • Management of isolated hypertriglyceridemia without elevated ASCVD risk.
  • Dyslipidemia management in children <10 years.

4. Policy

  • Requirements for coverage

5. Documentation requirements

  • Fasting lipid panel (LDL-C, non-HDL-C, HDL-C, TG, TC) within the past 3 months — minimum 2 values on different occasions to confirm persistent elevation.
  • Evidence of MTST ± ezetimibe for ≥3 months (or documented statin intolerance with ≥2 statin trials at different doses with symptom resolution after discontinuation).
  • ASCVD risk category documentation: clinical ASCVD diagnosis, FH diagnosis, or 10-year ASCVD risk estimate using PREVENT-ASCVD equations (per 2026 ACC/AHA) or PCE.
  • Specialist referral letter (cardiologist, lipidologist, or internal medicine specialist) confirming: risk category, therapy failure, proposed agent, and LDL-C target.
  • Documented lifestyle optimization: heart-healthy diet and physical activity counseling within the past 12 months.
  • Documented Lp(a) measurement at least once (Class I, 2026 ACC/AHA) — results must be available at time of advanced therapy request.

6. Coverage criteria - Pre-Treatment Investigations (Tiered Approach)

  • To avoid unnecessary cost burden while ensuring clinically appropriate agent selection, investigations are stratified into three coverage tiers:
  • 2 TIER 1 — Mandatory for ALL advanced lipid therapy coverage requests Requiredateverycoveragerequest,regardlessofagentrequested:
  • Fasting lipid panel: LDL-C (Martin/Hopkins preferred), non-HDL-C, HDL-C, TG, TC — ≥2 measurements on separate occasions at least 4 weeks apart.
  • Liver function tests (ALT/AST): baseline prior to initiation; required for ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and statin documentation.
  • Creatinine / eGFR: renal function affects risk category classification (CKD stage 3 = high risk, stage 4–5 = very high risk per Saudi 2022 guidelines).
  • Documentation of statin therapy history: agent, dose, duration, and tolerability. Minimum: MTST for ≥3 months, OR ≥2 documented statin trials with intolerance with symptom resolution after discontinuation.
  • PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk estimate (or equivalent: PCE, SCORE2) — for primary prevention patients only. Not required for known ASCVD or confirmed FH.
  • Lp(a) measurement: at least once per lifetime (Class I, 2026 ACC/AHA). Should be documented before approval of any advanced agent in primary prevention. If already measured and documented, repeat is not

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Overview:
  • Ganglion cysts are benign, fluid-filled masses arising from joints or tendon sheaths, most commonly in the wrist and hand. They often fluctuate in size and may resolve spontaneously. Management is symptom-driven, focusing
  • on functional limitation, pain, neurovascular compromise, or persistent patient discomfort. Evidence-based practice supports conservative management as first line, with surgical referral reserved for cases with recurrent
  • symptoms, mechanical interference, or confirmed structural impact. This guideline standardizes evaluation and intervention thresholds to ensure clinically appropriate, cost-aligned, and consistent decision-making.

2. Scope

  • This guideline covers the general diagnosis and treatment of ganglion cyst.

3. Policy

  • Diagnosis:
  • o Most ganglion cysts are clinical diagnosis with physical examination.
  • o Imaging: While radiographs are generally not helpful, an ultrasound or MRI can be useful for assessing the cyst's size, location, and relationship to surrounding structures, particularly in complex cases.
  • Management:
  • o Management is based on symptoms:
  • Asymptomatic ganglion cyst: Requires no intervention.
  • Mild to Moderate symptoms: Conservative therapy (Analgesia, Compression/Brace).
  • Severe: Surgical Treatment.
  • The conditions described below would be regarded as severe in this respect:
  • Ganglion on wrist with evidence of neurovascular compromise or significant pain.
  • Seed ganglia at base of digits with significant pain.
  • Mucoid cysts at the distal interphalangeal joint which has disrupted the nail growth or there are cysts that tend to discharge.
  • Ganglia on foot and ankles with evidence of neurovascular compromise or significant pain or causing difficulties with footwear or mobility.
  • Restriction of activities of daily living.
  • Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite initial treatment with conservative therapy.
  • Injection of ganglion cyst with glucocorticoids is not recommended.
  • Aspiration is not routinely recommended due to high recurrence rate.
  • Physiotherapy has no role in the treatment of ganglion cyst itself.
  • o Post-surgery Stiffness and decrease range of motion may occur which may require physiotherapy sessions (Up to 18 sessions)

2. Definitions

  • Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP): an acquired, immune-mediated neuropathy characterised by chronicity, demyelination and inflammation. In the classic form motor
  • involvement exceeds sensory. The course is slowly progressive in most patients, with a relapsing–remitting course in at least one-third. CIDP generally responds to immunomodulatory treatment with glucocorticoids,
  • IVIG or plasma exchange.
  • Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) and subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG): pooled human immunoglobulin used as an established first-line, disease-modifying therapy for CIDP; improvement is
  • usually detectable at two to six weeks.
  • Induction and maintenance treatment: induction is the initial treatment course given to achieve clinical improvement; maintenance is the ongoing therapy most patients require to sustain that improvement,
  • individualised over time to the lowest effective dose and longest interval.
  • Objective treatment response: improvement on at least one disability scale and at least one impairment scale — for example the Inflammatory Neuropathy Cause and Treatment (INCAT) disability scale, the
  • Inflammatory Rasch-built Overall Disability Scale (I-RODS), or the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score.

3. Scope

  • This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorization of Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG / SCIG) for children and adults with a confirmed diagnosis of chronic inflammatory demyelinating
  • polyradiculoneuropathy, in line with the CHI.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • IVIG for benign CIDP that manifests with only distal paraesthesiae and no significant functional impact — such patients may be monitored without immunomodulatory treatment.
  • IVIG for anti-MAG antibody–positive neuropathy (including anti-MAG positive DADS), which is considered distinct from CIDP, responds suboptimally to IVIG

4. Eligibility and Coverage Criteria

  • IVIG is covered as a first-line treatment (Level A) for a patient with a confirmed diagnosis of CIDP when both A and B are met::
  • A: Confirmed diagnosis of CIDP by a neurologist per EAN/PNS criteria, supported by nerve conduction studies demonstrating demyelination (and, where indicated, supportive CSF, imaging or biopsy findings).
  • AND
  • B: The neuropathy has a significant functional impact (not benign distal paraesthesiae alone).

5. Prescriber (MD) Requirement

  • IVIG must be prescribed by a neurologist.

6. Re-treatment

  • Maintenance IVIG is covered where an objective response to induction has been documented;
  • continuation without documented objective benefit at periodic review is not covered.
  • If there is no objective response after adequate induction (including the repeated 1 g/kg doses or a second 2 g/kg course), IVIG is considered ineffective and switching to an alternative first-line agent
  • (corticosteroids or plasma exchange, under their own policies) is appropriate.

7. Approved Dosing

  • Induction (adults): 2 g/kg total over 2–5 consecutive days (e.g. 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days); maximum 1 g/kg/day.
  • Inadequate first response: give 2–5 further doses of 1 g/kg every 3 weeks, or a second 2 g/kg course, before judging IVIG ineffective.
  • Maintenance (adults): start 1 g/kg every 3 weeks, then individualise to the lowest effective dose / longest interval (0.4–1 g/kg every 2–6 weeks); assess response after 2–3 months.
  • Review and taper: when stable, reduce ~25% per infusion, lengthen the interval, or discontinue — reviewed every 6–12 months for the first 2–3 years. If end-of-dose deterioration occurs, increase the dose
  • or shorten the interval.
  • Paediatric: no fixed dose — individualise to the lowest effective dose and taper gradually.
  • Weight: use adjusted body weight in obesity; avoid the 1 g/kg × 1–2 day regimen where fluid overload is a concern.

8. Selection of Agent

  • IVIG, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange are all first-line treatments for CIDP (Grade A). The guideline gives no overall preference between IVIG and corticosteroids, weakly prefers IVIG over plasma exchange.
  • For maintenance, subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) is strongly recommended and is a covered alternative to maintenance IVIG (weakly recommended against for induction); when switching from IVIG to SCIG, start
  • at the same mean weekly dose (1:1) and tailor to response.

9. Documentation Requirements

  • 1. Neurologist note confirming the diagnosis of CIDP (typical or specified variant), the duration of symptoms (at least eight weeks), and the supporting demyelinating electrodiagnostic findings (± CSF,
  • imaging or nerve biopsy where performed).
  • 2. Documentation of significant functional impact and the baseline disability / impairment scores (INCAT, I-RODS or MRC sum score) that will be used to judge treatment response; for maintenance requests, the
  • objective response to prior IVIG.
  • 3. Anti-MAG antibody status where an atypical distal (DADS) phenotype is present, to exclude anti-MAG neuropathy.
  • 4. Current weight (kg) — adjusted body weight where obese — for dose calculation, and baseline renal function (serum creatinine / eGFR).
  • 5. ICD-10 (G61.81) and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

documents.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) – IVIG
documents.rendered:
1. Definitions

  • Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS): Acute, usually monophasic immune-mediated polyneuropathy, often following an infection. IVIG and plasma exchange are effective immunotherapies.
  • Treatment-related fluctuation (TRF): Clinical deterioration after initial improvement following IVIG or plasma exchange; typically occurs within 10–60 days of starting treatment.
  • GBS Disability Score: Grade 1: minor symptoms, able to run. Grade 2: able to walk unaided but unable to run. Grade ≥3: unable to walk unaided, potentially bedbound.

2. Scope

  • Applies to children, adolescents and adults with confirmed GBS being assessed for IVIG treatment.
  • Excluded: corticosteroids for GBS; immediate sequential plasma exchange and IVIG; stable grade 1; stable grade 2 presenting more than 2 weeks after onset; routine switching of immunotherapy after treatment failure.

3. IVIG Eligibility and Coverage

  • Scenario 1 — Severe GBS: GBS-DS ≥3 (unable to walk unaided). Start IVIG within 4 weeks of symptom onset.
  • Scenario 2 — Ambulatory with poor prognostic features: Patient can walk but has rapid deterioration, respiratory involvement, bulbar weakness, autonomic disturbance or mEGOS ≥6. Start within 4 weeks.
  • Scenario 3 — Mild stable ambulatory GBS: GBS-DS 2, stable or slowly progressive. Arm weakness or cranial nerve involvement may support treatment. Start within 2 weeks only.
  • Ongoing deterioration more than 4 weeks after onset requires reassessment for acute-onset CIDP or an alternative diagnosis.

4. Re-treatment

  • Routine second IVIG course immediately after the first is not covered; no improved outcomes and increased adverse effects.
  • For documented TRF within the first 8 weeks after onset, retreatment using the initial modality is covered.
  • Switching between IVIG and plasma exchange solely for lack of improvement or deterioration is not covered.
  • Progression beyond 8 weeks or three or more fluctuations suggests acute-onset CIDP and requires diagnostic review.

5. Prescriber Requirements

  • Adults: consultant neurologist.
  • Children: pediatric neurologist or general pediatrician.

6. Approved Dosing

  • Adults and children: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg).
  • Children: alternative regimen 1 g/kg/day for 2 days (total 2 g/kg).
  • Use adjusted body weight for class I–III obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), as specified by the source guideline.

7. Selection of Agent

  • IVIG and plasma exchange have similar efficacy. When both are available without contraindications, IVIG is preferred because it is generally easier to administer and better tolerated.

8. Required Documentation

  • Specialist note confirming GBS, symptom-onset date and functional/disability grade.
  • Document non-ambulant status or poor prognostic features where applicable.
  • Current weight (adjusted weight if BMI ≥30), baseline creatinine/eGFR.
  • ICD-10 G61.0 and appropriately specific SBS codes.

9. Clinical Coverage Pathway

  • Confirm GBS → assess walking ability, disability grade, prognostic features and time from onset → verify applicable treatment window → verify prescriber, contraindications and documentation → assess IVIG coverage.
  • This is a reference pathway, not an automated authorization decision.

10. References

  • Council of Health Insurance (CHI). GBS Formulary Indication Review. December 2025.
  • van Doorn PA et al. EAN/PNS Guideline. J Peripher Nerv Syst. 2023;28:535–563. doi:10.1111/jns.12594.

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Human Immunoglobulin (IVIG) in Myasthenia Gravis

2. Definitions

  • Myasthenia gravis (MG): an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterised by fluctuating, fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, limb and/or respiratory muscles, caused by antibodies
  • directed against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or related proteins such as muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) or lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4).
  • MGFA clinical classification: the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America classification of disease severity (Classes I to V), used throughout this guideline as the primary severity metric for coverage decisions.
  • Table 1: MGFA clinical classification of myasthenia gravis severity Class Description Class I Ocular weakness only (ptosis and/or diplopia), with or without eyelid closure weakness; all other
  • muscle strength normal Class II Mild weakness of muscles other than ocular. IIa predominantly limb or axial; IIb predominantly oropharyngeal or respiratory
  • Class III Moderate weakness of muscles other than ocular. IIIa predominantly limb or axial; IIIb predominantly oropharyngeal or respiratory
  • Class IV Severe weakness of muscles other than ocular. IVa predominantly limb or axial; IVb predominantly oropharyngeal or respiratory (may include feeding tube without intubation)
  • Class V Intubation, with or without mechanical ventilation, except when used in routine postoperative

3. management

  • Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG): pooled human immunoglobulin G obtained from thousands of donors, used as a rapid-acting immunomodulatory therapy in MG. Clinical effect is usually seen within one
  • week and the benefit generally lasts three to six weeks.

4. Scope

  • This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of IVIG for children, adolescents and adults with a confirmed diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, in line with the CHI.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • Mild flares (isolated ptosis or diplopia, mild facial or limb weakness) that are manageable by adjusting pyridostigmine and/or the corticosteroid dose.
  • Concurrent or immediately sequential use of IVIG and plasma exchange for the same episode, which provides no additional benefit.
  • IVIG used as first-line chronic immunotherapy in stable, well-controlled disease, or in place of a corticosteroid and steroid-sparing agent in a patient who has no contraindication or intolerance to them.
  • Continuation of chronic IVIG beyond two treatment cycles in the absence of a documented objective clinical response.
  • Concurrent chronic IVIG together with an FcRn inhibitor, a complement C5 inhibitor or rituximab for the same patient, which constitutes therapeutic duplication.
  • Repeat courses requested on a fixed schedule without documentation of recurrent exacerbation or of maintained objective benefit.
  • MuSK-antibody positive MG, where plasma exchange and rituximab are the preferred options. IVIG remains covered for crisis and acute exacerbation but is not the preferred chronic therapy in MuSK
  • disease.

5. Eligibility and Coverage Criteria

  • IVIG is covered for a patient with an established diagnosis of MG when criterion A is met, AND at least one of criteria B, C, D or E is met:
  • A: Confirmed diagnosis of MG documented by a neurologist, supported by:
  • o Positive serum AChR antibody; or
  • o If AChR antibody is negative, a positive MuSK antibody; or
  • o a positive antibody result on a cell-based assay (for example clustered AChR or LRP4); or
  • o In seronegative patients, a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation and/or increased jitter on single-fibre electromyography, with a compatible clinical picture.
  • B: Myasthenic crisis — respiratory failure or severe bulbar weakness requiring ventilatory support or airway protection.
  • C: Acute exacerbation requiring a change in therapy — Significant worsening such as increasing dysphagia, dyspnoea or worsening bulbar or limb weakness, corresponding to MGFA class IIIb or higher, or an MG-
  • ADL increase of at least 3 points from the patient’s stable baseline, or a QMG score above 10.5.
  • D: Bridge therapy — To obtain rapid symptom control while a slower-acting immunotherapy (corticosteroid, steroid-sparing agent or rituximab) takes effect.
  • E: Refractory MG (chronic IVIG) — that remains inadequately controlled on optimised pyridostigmine and an adequate corticosteroid regimen, or where corticosteroid escalation is contraindicated or not tolerated.
  • Continuation and Re-authorisation:
  • Acute courses — are re-authorised for each documented recurrent exacerbation.
  • Chronic IVIG — is authorised initially for six months (approximately four to six cycles).
  • Re-authorisation of chronic IVIG — requires a documented improvement of at least 2 points on the MG-ADL or 3 points on the QMG compared with the pre-treatment baseline, together with evidence of
  • an attempted corticosteroid taper or infusion interval extension. Where these are met, a further twelve months may be authorised.

6. Documentation Requirements

  • 1. Neurologist note confirming the diagnosis and current severity/exacerbation.
  • 2. Antibody status and/or electrodiagnostic report.
  • 3. Current weight (kg) for dose calculation.
  • 4. Baseline renal function.
  • 5. ICD-10 and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

7. Approved Dosing

  • Parameter Detail Acute / rescue dose 2 g/kg per course, usually 0.4 g/kg/day over 2 to 5 days Administration Spread over more days in renal disease, congestive heart failure, thrombotic
  • risk or older adults Chronic / maintenance dose 1 to 2 g/kg every 4 to 6 weeks, individualised to the lowest effective dose Onset of effect Usually within 1 week
  • Duration of benefit Approximately 3 to 6 weeks Initial authorisation (chronic) 6 months; continuation requires MG-ADL improvement of at least 2 points

1. Definition

  • Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) comprises ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD), chronic immune- mediated disorders of the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Since there are no curative medical therapies, IBD is a non-communicable, chronic disease that needs lifelong treatment in the vast majority of cases.
  • Treatment may follow a traditional step-up approach, starting with mesalazine (UC only), followed by immunomodulators, then biologics; however, early biologic therapy may be appropriate in selected high-risk
  • patients.
  • Biologic therapies used for moderate-to-severe IBD include:
  • o Anti-TNF agents: infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab (UC only), certolizumab (CD only).
  • o Anti-integrin therapy: vedolizumab.
  • o Anti-IL-12/23 therapy: ustekinumab (Stelara).
  • o Anti-IL-23 therapy: risankizumab (CD only), mirikizumab (UC only).

2. Scope

  • This This guideline applies to insurance coverage decisions for biologic therapy in patients with confirmed moderate- to-severe inflammatory bowel disease.
  • This guideline does NOTcover:
  • Symptoms without confirmed IBD diagnosis.
  • Mild disease without poor prognostic factors: Biologic therapy for mild, non-progressive UC or CD that has not failed, and does not warrant bypassing, conventional therapy is not covered under this guideline.
  • Insufficient documentation: no disease severity, objective inflammation, prior treatment history, or treatment response.

3. Policy

  • Requirements for coverage:
  • Confirmed diagnosis: UC or CD must be supported by endoscopy, histology, radiology, or specialist documentation.
  • Disease severity: Evidence must show moderate-to-severe disease, based on symptoms, endoscopy, biomarkers, or hospitalization for acute severe disease.
  • Treatment history: Submission must show prior conventional therapy and response/failure/intolerance, or poor prognostic factors justifying upfront advanced therapy.
  • Approval Criteria:
  • 1. Moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis:
  • Biologic therapy may be approved when either of the following ulcerative colitis pathways is met:
  • 1. Mayo Score (Outpatient Pathway) Biologic therapy may be approved for patients with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis in the
  • outpatient setting if any of the following apply:
  • a. Total Mayo score of 6–12, with Mayo Endoscopic Subscore (MES) of 2 or 3.
  • Mayo score for UC Variable Definition Score Variable Definition Score Normal no. of daily bowel 0 Normal/inactive colitis 0 movements
  • 1–2 more bowel movements 1 Erythema, decreased vascularity 1 than normal Stool pattern Endoscopic findings 3–4 more bowel movements 2 Friability, marked erythema, 2
  • than normal erosions 5 or more bowel movements 3 Ulcerations, severe friability, 3 than normal spontaneous bleeding None 0 Normal 0
  • Blood streaks seen in the stool 1 Mild colitis 1 Most severe rectal Physician Global less than half of the time bleeding of the day Assessment
  • Blood in most stool 2 Moderate colitis 2 Pure blood passed 3 Severe colitis 3 b. Mild clinical symptoms but objective evidence of significant inflammatory burden and/or poor prognostic
  • features.
  • Any of the following features may predict a higher risk for long term sequelae (eg, colectomy):
  • Extensive colitis.
  • Deep colonic ulcers.
  • Age <40 years.
  • Elevated CRP and/or ESR.
  • Glucocorticoid requirement to maintain remission or Non-response or intolerance to an adequate trial
  • History of hospitalization for UC .
  • Co-existing infection (Clostridioidesdifficileinfection or cytomegalovirus infection) c. Glucocorticoid-dependent or refractory disease.
  • o Inability to taper corticosteroids without symptom recurrence, or failure to respond to an adequate corticosteroid course.
  • 1.2. Acute Severe Ulcerative Colitis (ASUC) Biologic therapy may be approved for patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) when the patient
  • meets Truelove and Witts criteria as:
  • ≥6 bloody bowel movements per day PLUS at least ONE of the following systemic toxicity features (all four are not required simultaneously):
  • Fever > 37.8°C (100°F)
  • Tachycardia > 90 beats per minute
  • Anemia: Hemoglobin < 10.5 g/dL
  • Elevated ESR > 30 mm/hr or elevated CRP (CRP ≥12 mg/L has been suggested as a sensitive cut-off for determining UC severity.) KeyPearl:
  • Repeat endoscopy is not mandatory before biologic approval when ulcerative colitis and prior active endoscopic disease have already been documented. Previous endoscopic findings may be accepted in conjunction with current clinical and
  • objective evidence of active inflammation (e.g., fecal calprotectin and/or CRP). Repeat endoscopy should be requested when disease activity is uncertain, available documentation is inadequate, or endoscopic reassessment is clinically
  • indicated.
  • 2. Moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease Moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease may be defined by validated disease activity scores and/or high-risk features,
  • with objective evidence of active inflammation.
  • 2.1: As per Clinical scoring systems Clinical scoring systems include the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and the Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI).
  • CDAI:
  • 220–450: moderate disease
  • >450: severe disease Calculator: https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/3318/crohns-disease-activity-index-cdai HBI:
  • 8-16: moderate activity
  • >16 indicates severe activity.
  • Calculator: https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/10069/harvey-bradshaw-index-hbi-crohns-disease The HBI is a simplified version of the CDAI to collect clinical data related to CD.
  • The index includes five parameters:
  • 1. Patient well-being for the previous day (very well = 0, slightly below par = 1, poor = 2, very poor = 3, terrible = 4) 2. Abdominal pain for the previous day (none = 0, mild = 1, moderate = 2, severe = 3)
  • 3. Number of liquid or soft stools for the previous day 4. Abdominal mass (none = 0, dubious = 1, definite = 2, definite and tender = 3)
  • 5. Complications (none = 0, yes = 1 point for each: arthralgia, uveitis, erythema nodosum, aphthous ulcer, pyoderma gangrenosum, anal fissures, appearance of a new fistula, abscess)
  • 2.1: High-risk features (moderate to severe Crohn)
  • Diagnosis at a younger age (<30 years)
  • History of active or recent tobacco use
  • Elevated C-reactive protein and/or fecal calprotectin levels
  • Deep ulcers on colonoscopy
  • Long segments of small and/or large bowel involvement
  • Perianal disease
  • Extra-intestinal manifestations
  • History of bowel resections
  • Patients who have not responded to glucocorticoids (ie, refractory) or who relapse after achieving clinical remission following induction therapy with glucocorticoids

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Comprehensive EMG/NCS Medical Necessity Guideline Region: Saudi Arabia Language: English Version: 1.0 Purpose of this Document evidence-based decisions regarding approval or rejection of requests for Nerve Conduction
  • Studies (NCS) and Electromyography (EMG). It summarizes the clinical role of these tests, defines appropriate and inappropriate indications, and offers practical decision tools,
  • examples, and checklists tailored to the workflow of an insurance medical department.
  • Although the primary focus is on neurology requests, many of the principles also apply to requests from orthopedics, neurosurgery, physical medicine and rehabilitation, and other
  • specialties.

2. 1. Background and General Principles

  • NCS and EMG are specialized neurophysiologic tests used to evaluate the function of peripheral nerves, nerve roots, neuromuscular junctions, and muscles. They provide

3. objective information that can confirm or refute a suspected diagnosis, characterize the

  • severity and distribution of a disorder, and help guide treatment decisions. However, these tests are resource-intensive and should be reserved for situations in which the results are
  • likely to influence patient management.
  • From the payer perspective, it is crucial to ensure that EMG/NCS are used appropriately.
  • Overuse leads to increased costs without meaningful benefit, while underuse may delay diagnosis of significant neurologic conditions. The key concept of medical necessity is
  • therefore central to this guideline. A test is medically necessary when:
  • The clinical evaluation alone is insufficient to confirm or exclude an important suspected

4. diagnosis; and

  • The result of the test will reasonably be expected to change management, such as confirming a diagnosis, ruling out serious disease, guiding surgical decisions, or altering
  • medication or rehabilitation plans.
  • 2. Overview of NCS and EMG Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) measure how quickly and strongly electrical signals travel along peripheral nerves. These tests assess large myelinated fibers and are particularly
  • useful for detecting focal entrapment neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome, generalized polyneuropathies such as diabetic neuropathy, and focal mononeuropathies
  • such as radial or peroneal nerve palsies.
  • Electromyography (EMG) involves inserting a fine needle electrode into selected muscles to assess their electrical activity at rest and during voluntary contraction. EMG is especially
  • important for evaluating radiculopathies, plexopathies, motor neuron disease (such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), and myopathic processes. In clinical practice, NCS and EMG
  • are frequently performed together as a combined study, and this guideline treats them as a unified service unless otherwise specified.
  • 3. General Indications by Symptom Category Medical reviewers will frequently see EMG/NCS requests framed around one or more symptoms: numbness, tingling, pain, weakness, gait disturbance, or abnormal movements.
  • The presence, pattern, and progression of these symptoms, combined with the neurological examination, are critical in determining whether testing is warranted.
  • 3.1 Numbness and Tingling (Paresthesia) EMG/NCS may be indicated when numbness or tingling:
  • Follows a clear peripheral nerve or dermatomal distribution (for example, median nerve involvement in the first three digits of the hand);
  • Has persisted for at least 4–6 weeks despite conservative measures;
  • Is associated with objective sensory loss on examination or functional impairment such as dropping objects or difficulty with fine motor tasks;
  • Is unilateral or markedly asymmetric, raising concern for focal entrapment or radiculopathy; or
  • Occurs in a patient with diabetes or other systemic risk factors where there is concern for superimposed focal neuropathy or atypical neuropathy.
  • Testing is usually not indicated when paresthesia is diffuse, intermittent, clearly related to anxiety or hyperventilation, or when there is a completely normal neurologic examination
  • and no impact on function.
  • 3.2 Weakness Objective weakness is one of the strongest indications for EMG/NCS. Reviewers should look for documentation that demonstrates true loss of strength rather than fatigue or subjective
  • heaviness. EMG/NCS are typically appropriate when there is:
  • Focal limb weakness suggestive of a mononeuropathy or radiculopathy (for example, foot drop, wrist drop, difficulty with ankle dorsiflexion, or loss of shoulder abduction);
  • Progressive or unexplained proximal weakness raising concern for myopathy or neuromuscular junction disease;
  • Asymmetrical weakness in a patient with known polyneuropathy where an additional focal lesion is suspected; or
  • Rapidly progressive weakness affecting respiratory or bulbar muscles, which may require urgent evaluation.
  • EMG/NCS are usually not indicated when the only complaint is generalized fatigue, mild subjective weakness without any abnormal findings on examination, or weakness clearly
  • explained by non-neurologic conditions such as severe pain, joint disease, or deconditioning.
  • 3.3 Pain Pain alone is a weak indication for EMG/NCS. These tests should not be used as a general screening tool for chronic pain. However, they may be appropriate when pain is
  • accompanied by neurological signs or follows a specific neurologic pattern. EMG/NCS may be approved when:
  • There is radicular pain (neck or back pain radiating down an arm or leg) lasting more than 6 weeks despite conservative therapy, especially when accompanied by weakness, reflex
  • asymmetry, or dermatomal sensory loss;
  • There is focal limb pain in a distribution that strongly suggests entrapment neuropathy; or
  • There is suspicion of complex regional pain syndrome or nerve injury following trauma or surgery and the result will change management.
  • EMG/NCS should generally be rejected for nonspecific low back pain, fibromyalgia, mechanical joint pain, and other pain syndromes without evidence of neurologic
  • involvement.

5. 4. Indications by Disease Category

  • Reviewers may also encounter EMG/NCS requests linked to specific suspected or established diagnoses. The following subsections outline conditions where testing is
  • typically appropriate, conditionally appropriate, or usually not necessary.
  • 4.1 Entrapment Neuropathies Common examples include carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head, and tarsal tunnel syndrome. EMG/NCS are usually
  • indicated when:
  • There is a consistent history of focal numbness, tingling, or weakness in the distribution of a specific nerve;
  • Symptoms have persisted beyond 4–6 weeks or have not responded to initial conservative

6. treatment such as splinting or activity modification; and

  • Surgical decompression is being considered and objective confirmation is required.
  • 4.2 Radiculopathies In suspected cervical or lumbar radiculopathy, EMG/NCS can support the diagnosis and help differentiate radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy or plexopathy. Appropriate

7. indications include

  • Radiating limb pain in a dermatomal pattern lasting more than 6 weeks;
  • Weakness in muscles innervated by the suspected root; and
  • Abnormal reflexes or sensory loss consistent with the suspected root level.
  • If high-quality imaging (such as MRI) and the clinical picture already clearly support the

8. diagnosis and no change in management is expected based on EMG findings, testing may be

  • unnecessary.
  • 4.3 Polyneuropathies For patients with suspected generalized peripheral neuropathy, EMG/NCS are often the most informative tests. They help distinguish axonal from demyelinating processes and
  • guide further investigations. Testing is generally appropriate when:
  • There is length-dependent sensory loss, starting in the feet and potentially progressing to the hands;
  • Reflexes are reduced or absent distally;
  • There is weakness in distal muscles; or
  • There is concern for rapidly progressive or inflammatory neuropathy.
  • 4.4 Myopathies EMG is a valuable tool in the evaluation of primary muscle disease. Approval may be appropriate for patients with:
  • Symmetric proximal weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, or lifting arms overhead);
  • Elevated creatine kinase or other evidence of muscle involvement; and
  • Family history or clinical suspicion of inherited myopathy or inflammatory myositis.
  • 4.5 Motor Neuron Disease and ALS When clinicians suspect amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or another motor neuron disease, EMG is essential for confirming the diagnosis and excluding mimics. EMG/NCS should be
  • approved in the presence of:
  • Progressive weakness affecting multiple regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral);
  • Upper and lower motor neuron signs on examination; or
  • Fasciculations, muscle atrophy, and unexplained weight loss.
  • 5. Situations Where EMG/NCS Are Usually Not Indicated Medical reviewers should feel confident rejecting EMG/NCS requests when the clinical
  • scenario does not support neurologic testing or when results will not change management.
  • Common low-value indications include:
  • Diffuse musculoskeletal pain without neurologic deficits;
  • Fibromyalgia and other centralized pain syndromes;
  • Chronic low back pain without radiation, sensory changes, or weakness;
  • Subjective numbness or tingling with completely normal neurological examination and no functional limitation;
  • Follow-up of a stable, well-characterized neuropathy without any change in symptoms;
  • Repeat EMG/NCS within 6 months of a previous study unless there is clear documentation of new or rapidly progressive deficits.
  • 6. Required Documentation for Approval To approve EMG/NCS, reviewers should expect a minimum standard of documentation in the request. The following elements are strongly recommended:
  • A clear statement of the main symptom(s) and duration (for example, 'right hand numbness for 3 months' or 'progressive left foot drop over 6 weeks');
  • Relevant neurological examination findings, including muscle strength grades, sensory changes, reflex findings, and presence of atrophy or fasciculations;
  • Clinical differential diagnosis or working diagnosis (for example, 'suspected L5 radiculopathy' or 'rule out carpal tunnel syndrome versus cervical radiculopathy');
  • Description of any prior investigations that relate to the request, such as MRI of the spine or brain, and whether the results are concordant or discordant with the clinical findings;
  • Documentation of previous conservative management and response (physiotherapy, splinting, medications);
  • The specialty of the requesting physician, with neurology, neurosurgery, or physical medicine and rehabilitation typically providing the most detailed neurodiagnostic rationale.
  • 7. Stepwise Reviewer Decision Algorithm A simple, repeatable approach can help reviewers reach consistent decisions. The following

9. algorithm can be applied to most EMG/NCS requests

  • Step 1 – Confirm the primary symptom and its duration.
  • If symptoms have lasted less than 4–6 weeks and there are no red flags, consider suggesting continued conservative management before testing.
  • Step 2 – Look for objective neurological findings.
  • Approvals should generally require at least one documented abnormal neurological sign (weakness, sensory loss, reflex change, atrophy, or fasciculations).
  • Step 3 – Assess whether the clinical picture suggests a focal or generalized neurologic problem.
  • Focal deficits (single nerve or root distribution) or clear length-dependent neuropathy are more likely to benefit from testing.
  • Step 4 – Ask whether EMG/NCS will change management.
  • If the treating physician clearly explains that results will guide surgery, confirm diagnosis, or differentiate between two competing conditions, testing is more likely to be justified.
  • Step 5 – Check for recent prior EMG/NCS.
  • Avoid approving repeat testing within 6 months unless new deficits or major clinical changes are documented.
  • 8. High-Priority and Automatically Approved Scenarios Certain clinical scenarios carry a high risk of serious neurologic disease and should
  • generally be approved without delay:
  • New-onset foot drop or wrist drop with supporting examination findings;
  • Rapidly progressive limb weakness over days to weeks;
  • Suspected Guillain–Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy);
  • Suspected motor neuron disease (ALS) with appropriate clinical features;
  • Severe radicular symptoms with objective deficits where surgery is being considered;
  • Suspected neuromuscular junction disorders causing fatigable weakness or respiratory compromise.
  • 9. Case-Based Examples for Reviewers Case 1 – Appropriate Request A 52-year-old woman with diabetes presents with progressive numbness and tingling in the
  • first three digits of her right hand for 4 months. She reports dropping objects and nocturnal symptoms. Examination reveals reduced sensation in the median nerve distribution and
  • mild weakness of thumb abduction. The neurologist requests EMG/NCS to confirm carpal tunnel syndrome and assess severity before considering surgery. This is an appropriate
  • indication and should be approved.
  • Case 2 – Inappropriate Request A 40-year-old man presents with diffuse back pain for 2 years. There is no radiation of pain, no numbness or weakness, and neurological examination is normal. The physician requests
  • EMG/NCS 'to rule out nerve damage.' There is no clear neurologic indication, and results are unlikely to change management. This request should be rejected.
  • Case 3 – Borderline Request A 60-year-old woman reports intermittent tingling in both hands for 2 weeks, worse at night. Neurological examination is normal. The physician requests EMG/NCS immediately.
  • In this scenario, conservative treatment with wrist splints and observation is reasonable before testing. Reviewers may reasonably reject or defer approval pending a trial of
  • conservative management and reassessment if symptoms persist or progress.
  • 10. Reviewer Checklist Before approving EMG/NCS, reviewers should answer 'yes' to most of the following questions:
  • Is there a clearly stated clinical question or suspected diagnosis?
  • Are there documented objective neurologic findings?
  • Have symptoms persisted for at least 4–6 weeks (except in urgent cases)?
  • Is the condition one in which EMG/NCS are known to be helpful (for example, entrapment neuropathy, radiculopathy, polyneuropathy, myopathy, motor neuron disease)?
  • Is it likely that test results will change management?
  • Has unnecessary repeat testing been avoided?
  • EMG and NCS are valuable diagnostic tools when used in the right clinical context. For low-value or unnecessary studies. By focusing on symptom duration, objective neurologic
  • findings, appropriate disease categories, and a clear link between test results and

10. management decisions, reviewers can make balanced, consistent, and defensible

  • determinations.
  • This guideline is intended to be a living document. As new evidence emerges and as local practice patterns evolve, it may be updated or expanded. Feedback from reviewers and
  • clinicians is encouraged to improve clarity, applicability, and ease of use in daily decision- making.

1. Clinical Guidance

  • Precocious Puberty

2. Definitions

  • Precocious puberty: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 years in girls (breast development, Tanner B2) or before age 9 years in boys (testicular volume ≥4 mL), confirmed on physical examination.
  • Central precocious puberty (CPP): GnRH-dependent ("true") precocious puberty caused by premature activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis resulting in progressive pubertal development with pubertal
  • gonadotropin secretion. Could be idiopathic or secondary to central nervous system pathology.
  • Peripheral precocious puberty (PPP): GnRH-independent ("pseudo-") precocious puberty resulting from an autonomous source of sex steroids (ovarian, testicular, adrenal, exogenous, or hCG-secreting tumor) with suppressed
  • basal and stimulated gonadotropins.
  • Progressive puberty: Documented advancement of pubertal (Tanner) staging, accelerated linear growth velocity, and/or bone age advancement on serial assessment. Rapid progression is defined as advancement to Tanner B3
  • within 6 months of the onset of thelarche.
  • Non-progressive premature thelarche: Isolated, typically stable or slowly regressing breast development, most common under age 3 years, without other pubertal signs, without significant growth acceleration, and without
  • significant bone age advancement.
  • Premature adrenarche: Isolated early appearance of pubic and/or axillary hair and adult-type body odor due to early adrenal androgen production, without breast development (girls) or testicular enlargement (boys), and without
  • significant growth acceleration.
  • Bone age advancement: Skeletal (bone) age, assessed by the Greulich-Pyle atlas on a left hand-wrist radiograph, significantly greater than chronological age — a key indicator of sex-steroid exposure and a determinant of predicted
  • adult height.
  • Tanner staging: Standardized five-stage classification (Tanner I–V) of breast development and pubic hair in girls, and genital development and pubic hair in boys, used to document pubertal onset and progression.

3. Scope

  • Included:
  • Children referred for evaluation of suspected precocious puberty.
  • Confirmed central precocious puberty (CPP).
  • Confirmed peripheral precocious puberty (PPP).
  • Monitoring of approved GnRH-agonist therapy and continuation/discontinuation decisions.
  • Excluded:
  • Isolated, non-progressive premature thelarche.
  • Isolated premature adrenarche.
  • Normal pubertal timing variants (including constitutional/familial early normal puberty).
  • Delayed puberty.
  • Adult endocrine disorders and adult reproductive endocrinology.

4. Policy

  • Requirements for coverage

5. Documentation Requirements

  • Patient age and sex
  • Growth chart (height, weight, BMI plotted against age- and sex-specific percentiles).
  • Height velocity (cm/year), calculated from at least two measurements 3–6 months apart.
  • Pubertal (Tanner) staging, with date of onset and serial findings if available.
  • Additional requirements for treatment (GnRH agonist or peripheral-precocity therapy) requests:
  • Bone-age report (radiograph and interpretation).
  • Basal LH (and FSH) results.
  • Estradiol (girls) or testosterone (boys).
  • GnRH/GnRH-agonist stimulation test result, if performed (required when basal LH is discordant with clinical picture).
  • Details of any previous treatment (agent, dose, duration, response).
  • Written recommendation from Pediatric Endocrinologist for pharmacologic treatment.
  • For suspected peripheral precocity: relevant imaging (pelvic/testicular ultrasound, adrenal imaging), adrenal steroid panel, or karyotype as applicable to the suspected etiology.

6. Coverage Criteria — Investigation

  • First: Approve routinely (once diagnostic evaluation is clinically indicated):
  • Basal LH, FSH, Estradiol (girls) or testosterone (boys).
  • Bone age radiograph (Left hand/wrist) Second: Approve only when indicated:
  • Clinical Indication Investigation when initial labs are discordant with the clinical picture (i.e., ongoing GnRH/GnRH-agonist (e.g., leuprolide) stimulation test.
  • pubertal progression with low prepubertal basal LH) Peripheral precocity suspected, in girls to assess uterine/ovarian Pelvic ultrasound volume and exclude ovarian cyst/tumor
  • Peripheral precocity suspected, in boys with asymmetric testicular Testicular ultrasound enlargement— to exclude gonadal tumor.
  • Pubic hair with signs of androgen excess (acne, clitoromegaly, rapid 17-hydroxyprogesterone, DHEAS, androstenedione virilization), suspected congenital adrenal hyperplasia
  • Boys with peripheral precocious puberty or suspected hCG-secreting Serum hCG germ-cell tumor Suspected primary hypothyroidism TSH, free T4
  • Any CNS signs/symptoms regardless of age; girls <6 years or boys Brain MRI <9 years with confirmed CPP; rapidly progressive CPP.

7. Coverage Criteria — Treatment

  • GnRH agonist therapy for central precocious puberty:

8. Treatment is medically necessary when ALL the following are present

  • 1. Age: Girl < 8 years. Boys < 9 years 2. Evidence of progressive Puberty:
  • Advancement in Tanner stage within 3-6 months
  • Accelerated height velocity (>6 cm/year)
  • Advanced bone age (>2 years above chronological age)

9. 3. Laboratory confirmation

  • Basal LH ≥ pubertal range Or
  • Pubertal response on GnRH stimulation test 4. Pediatric endocrinologist recommendation Special Consideration: Rapidly Progressive Puberty After the Age Cut-off
  • For puberty starting at ≥8 years in girls or ≥9 years in boys, GnRH-agonist treatment is not routinely indicated based on age or rapid progression alone.

10. Treatment may be considered on an individualized basis when ALL the following are present

  • Rapid pubertal progression: Tanner-stage advancement within 3–6 months and/or accelerated growth velocity (>6 cm/year).
  • Advanced bone age: preferably ≥2 years above chronological age or significant advancement on serial assessment.
  • Compromised height potential: predicted adult height (PAH) below or progressively declining relative to mid-parental/target height.
  • Confirmed central puberty: pubertal basal LH or pubertal response to GnRH/GnRH-agonist stimulation.
  • Pediatric Endocrinologist recommendation, documenting the expected benefit of GnRH-agonist treatment.
  • Rapid Tanner progression or advanced bone age alone is insufficient for treatment approval.
  • Do NOT approve GnRH-agonist treatment when:
  • Puberty is slowly progressive (ie. no change in Tanner (breast/genital/pubic hair) stage over ≥6 months of observation) — these children generally reach target adult height without treatment and girls with slow
  • progression typically experience menarche at a normal age (~11 years) untreated.
  • Predicted adult height approximates mid-parental target height — a conservative (no-treatment) approach is appropriate regardless of chronological age.

11. Treatment for Peripheral precocious puberty: (Cause-Directed)

  • Cause Approved treatment approach Gonadal (testicular/ovarian) tumor, hCG-secreting germ- Surgical resection; radiation/chemotherapy for hCG-secreting tumors as indicated.
  • cell tumor, adrenal tumor Conservative clinical monitoring with serial exam/ultrasound to document spontaneous Functioning ovarian
  • regression; surgery is not routinely indicated. If no regression, re-image to exclude alternative follicular cyst pathology (e.g., granulosa cell tumor).
  • Exogenous sex-steroid Identify and remove the exposure source; no pharmacologic treatment routinely required — exposure pubertal changes are expected to regress.
  • Cause Approved treatment approach Classic congenital adrenal Glucocorticoid replacement (endocrinologist-directed). hyperplasia GnRH-agonist therapy is indicated only if secondary (superimposed) central precocity subsequently develops —
  • patients being treated for peripheral precocity should be monitored clinically for signs of progressive breast/testicular development for at least 6 months after the primary cause is treated.

  • may switch to a 3-month preparation once suppression is achieved.

  • month 45 mg data than 1- and 3-month formulations.

  • 50 mg subcutaneous implant, surgically Suppression may last longer than 12 months in Histrelin acetate implant inserted/removed; approved for 12 months
  • practice. of use (children ≥2 years) Continuation Criteria:
  • Continued approval requires ALL the following:
  • Ongoing Pediatric Endocrinology follow-up, generally every 3–6 months.
  • Clinical evidence of pubertal suppression: stabilization or regression of secondary sexual characteristics, no new progression in Tanner stage.
  • Growth velocity normalizing toward pre-pubertal, age-appropriate rate.
  • Bone age advancement appropriately slowing on interval imaging.

12. Monitoring

  • Clinical monitoring (every 3-6 months):
  • Pubertal development (Tanner stage) and growth velocity. Effective therapy should show cessation of further breast/testicular development and menses, with declining height velocity.
  • Vaginal bleeding (girls): expected transiently within the first weeks of therapy due to estradiol withdrawal;
  • if it occurs later in treatment, this indicates incomplete suppression or an alternative diagnosis and should prompt reassessment.

13. Laboratory Monitoring: Areaofclinicalpracticevariation

  • Routine biochemical monitoring (basal or stimulated LH, estradiol/testosterone) is NOT required to approve continuation in a patient with clear clinical suppression/ or adequate bone-age response.
  • Where the treating physician's standard protocol includes periodic biochemical suppression testing, or where there is clinical evidence of ongoing pubertal progression on treatment (to confirm suppression and
  • guide dose/interval adjustment), such testing should be approved.
  • Radiology monitoring:
  • Bone age: approximately every 6–12 months initially, to confirm a reduction in the rate of bone age advancement; once this is documented, frequency may be reduced to every 1–2 years.
  • Repeat brain MRI only if new CNS signs/symptoms develop; not on a routine interval basis.
  • Discontinuation Criteria
  • Treatment is generally continued to approximately age 11 years in girls and age 12 years in boys.
  • Individualized by the treating endocrinologist based on height, bone age, psychosocial readiness, and peer- concordant pubertal timing.
  • Discontinuation is a clinical decision; If therapy is requested beyond the typical stopping age range, request the endocrinologist's specific justification.
