1. Definitions

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): a chronic inflammatory arthritis characterised by synovitis that predominantly affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet in a symmetric distribution.
  • Synovitis: joint inflammation demonstrated on physical examination, or, where the physical examination is inconclusive, on ultrasonography or magnetic resonance imaging. Joint pain in the absence of synovitis does
  • not constitute synovitis.
  • Rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA): the two RA-associated autoantibodies. ACPA is measured in clinical practice as the anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP)
  • antibody. A high positive result is a titre above three times the upper limit of normal; a low positive result is a titre above the upper limit of normal but not exceeding three times that limit.
  • Acute phase reactants: the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and the C-reactive protein (CRP).
  • Seronegative RA: RA in which both RF and ACPA are negative. Both are negative at presentation in up to 50 percent of patients and remain negative during follow-up in 20 percent.
  • Felty syndrome (FS): RA with persistent neutropenia, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below 2,000/microL that is not explained by concurrent illness or drug therapy, usually with splenomegaly.

2. Scope

  • This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of laboratory testing performed for the diagnosis and classification of RA, for the monitoring of RA disease activity, and for the assessment of extra-
  • articular and comorbid disease in adults.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • Laboratory testing performed for the safety monitoring of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, biologic agents, Janus kinase inhibitors or glucocorticoids, which is governed by the companion guideline on
  • laboratory monitoring of therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and any patient below 18 years of age.
  • Multi-biomarker disease activity testing, including the Vectra DA score.
  • Anti-mutated citrullinated vimentin (anti-MCV) antibodies, serum 14-3-3eta and anti-carbamylated protein (anti-CarP) antibodies.
  • Human leukocyte antigen typing and any other genetic or pharmacogenetic testing for the diagnosis of RA.
  • Serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6), matrix metalloproteinases, interferon gamma-induced protein 10, anti-citrullinated heat shock protein 90 antibodies and leukocyte telomere length.
  • High-sensitivity CRP performed for cardiovascular risk stratification.

3. Policy

  • Serologic Testing for the Diagnosis of RA:
  • RF, ACPA and one or both acute phase reactants are covered once where both of the following are met:
  • A: Synovitis is present in at least one joint; AND
  • B: No alternative diagnosis better explains the synovitis.
  • RF and ACPA are not covered in patients with joint pain in the absence of synovitis, including nonspecific arthralgia, fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis, and are not covered as a screening test in asymptomatic individuals.
  • Where a documented RF or ACPA result already exists, a repeat measurement of that antibody is not covered.
  • CBC, serum creatinine and aminotransferases are covered once at the time of diagnosis.
  • The following non-laboratory investigations are covered as part of the diagnostic assessment:
  • Plain radiographs: of the hands and wrists and an anteroposterior view of both forefeet, once at diagnosis.
  • Ultrasonography: of the affected joints where synovitis cannot be determined on physical examination, or magnetic resonance imaging where ultrasonography is not available.

4. Laboratory Monitoring of Disease Activity

  • ESR and/or CRP are covered at each disease assessment, at the following intervals:
  • Every 3 months while disease is active, until the patient is stable in remission or in low disease activity.
  • Every 3 to 6 months once remission or low disease activity is sustained.
  • At any additional visit prompted by a documented disease flare, a change of therapy or a dose increase.
  • CBC, serum creatinine and aminotransferases obtained for drug safety monitoring under the companion guideline are not separately covered as disease-activity tests.
  • In patients treated with an interleukin 6 receptor inhibitor or a Janus kinase inhibitor, a normal ESR or CRP does not establish remission, and a composite disease activity measure that contains no acute phase reactant
  • is required to document treatment response.
  • Repeat plain radiographs, ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging are not covered for routine disease-activity monitoring, and are covered only where there is clinical evidence of disease progression or
  • the joint examination is equivocal.
  • Suspected Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease:
  • In a patient with RA and respiratory symptoms, abnormal pulmonary function testing or a chest radiograph suggesting diffuse parenchymal disease, the following are covered:
  • CBC with differential.
  • Serum natriuretic peptide.
  • Antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, a myositis antibody panel and cryoglobulins are covered only where purpura, Raynaud phenomenon, skin ulcers or renal disease is documented.
  • ESR and CRP are not covered for the evaluation of lung disease.
  • Suspected Felty Syndrome:
  • Where a patient with RA has an ANC below 2,000/microL on at least two occasions and drug-induced neutropenia has been excluded, the following are covered:
  • CBC with differential white blood cell count.
  • Peripheral blood smear review with immunophenotypic analysis, to exclude large granular lymphocyte leukaemia.
  • RF and ACPA, where no result is already documented.
  • Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy with immunophenotypic and clonality analysis, where analysis of the peripheral blood is insufficient to exclude leukaemia.
  • Antihistone antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and anti-glucose-6-phosphate isomerase antibodies are not covered for the diagnosis of Felty syndrome, and serum Fc-gamma RIII and granulocyte
  • colony-stimulating factor concentrations are not covered.
  • Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:
  • A fasting lipid panel comprising total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein and triglycerides is covered as an input to a validated cardiovascular risk calculator, on the same terms as in the
  • general population.

5. Documentation Requirements

  • Treating physician note describing the joints examined and the presence of synovitis, or the ultrasonographic or magnetic resonance findings relied on.
  • For diagnostic serology, confirmation that no previous RF or ACPA result is available.
  • For disease-activity monitoring, the established diagnosis of RA, the current therapy and the date of the last covered acute phase reactant.
  • For extra-articular testing, the clinical finding that triggers the test, being the respiratory finding, the documented ANC or the clinical feature listed above.
  • ICD-10 and SBS codes coded to the highest level of specificity and accuracy.

1. Definitions

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): a chronic inflammatory arthritis characterised by synovitis that predominantly affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet in a symmetric distribution.
  • Conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (csDMARD): methotrexate (MTX), leflunomide (LEF), sulfasalazine (SSZ), hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) and azathioprine (AZA).
  • Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (bDMARD): the tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab pegol and golimumab; abatacept; rituximab; and the
  • interleukin 6 (IL-6) receptor inhibitors tocilizumab and sarilumab.
  • Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor: tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib.
  • Pre-treatment screening: laboratory testing obtained before the first dose of an agent to establish safety of initiation and a baseline for later monitoring.

2. Scope

  • This guideline governs the medical necessity and pre-authorisation of laboratory testing performed for the safety monitoring of csDMARD, bDMARD, JAK inhibitor and glucocorticoid therapy in adults with RA.
  • This guideline does NOT cover:
  • Laboratory testing for the diagnosis and classification of RA, for the monitoring of RA disease activity and for the assessment of extra-articular and comorbid disease, which is governed by the companion
  • guideline on laboratory testing in rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and any patient below 18 years of age.
  • The medicines themselves, which are governed by the pharmacy benefit.
  • Leflunomide and teriflunomide concentrations measured to assess efficacy or adherence.
  • Cytochrome P450 (CYP1A2) and dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) genotyping before leflunomide.
  • NAT2, HLA-B*08:01 and HLA-A*31:01 genotyping before sulfasalazine.
  • Red cell 6-thioguanine metabolite levels during azathioprine therapy.
  • B-cell or CD19 counts during rituximab therapy.

3. Policy

  • Laboratory testing listed in this guideline is covered where the patient has an established diagnosis of RA and is starting, or is established on, the agent concerned. Covered intervals are summarised in Table 1.
  • General Pre-Treatment Screening:
  • The following is covered once before the first dose of any csDMARD, bDMARD or JAK inhibitor:
  • CBC.
  • Serum creatinine.
  • Aminotransferases.
  • ESR and CRP.
  • Hepatitis B serology comprising HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc, and hepatitis C serology.
  • Repeat general pre-treatment screening is not covered when a subsequent agent is started.
  • Hepatitis B and hepatitis C serology may be repeated only where a new exposure is documented.
  • In a patient with serologic evidence of prior hepatitis B infection, an HBV viral load is covered every 6 to 12 months for the duration of therapy.
  • Additional Pre-Treatment Screening by Agent:
  • Before any bDMARD or JAK inhibitor. Latent tuberculosis screening. Repeat screening is covered where the patient is at increased risk of tuberculosis, has a documented exposure, or has been treated for latent
  • tuberculosis with potential ongoing exposure. Chest radiograph, where the patient has risk factors for latent tuberculosis, including where the screening test is negative.
  • Before a JAK inhibitor. CBC with differential and platelet count; serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen and eGFR; ALT, AST, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; a lipid panel; and serum hCG in females of
  • reproductive age.
  • Before an IL-6 receptor inhibitor. CBC with differential and platelet count; ALT, AST, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; a lipid panel; and serum hCG in females of reproductive age.
  • Before rituximab. HIV serology and serum immunoglobulins IgG, IgM and IgA. Chest radiograph, where one has not been obtained within the previous six months.
  • Before sulfasalazine. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) assay, where the patient belongs to a population at high risk of G6PD deficiency, which includes groups originating from the Middle East and the
  • Mediterranean region.
  • Before methotrexate or leflunomide, Chest radiograph.
  • Before hydroxychloroquine, Complete ophthalmologic examination, covered within the first year of therapy.
  • Conventional Synthetic DMARDs:
  • Methotrexate, Leflunomide and Sulfasalazine, a CBC, aminotransferases and serum creatinine are covered, with serum albumin for methotrexate:
  • Every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months of therapy and after any dose increase.
  • Every 8 to 12 weeks for months 3 to 6.
  • Every 12 weeks thereafter.
  • Sulfasalazine, a CBC is additionally covered one week after each dose increase.
  • Methotrexate and Leflunomide given in combination, a CBC, serum creatinine, albumin and transaminases are covered every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months and after any dose increase, every 4 weeks for the next
  • 3 months, then every 3 months.
  • Leflunomide, where the ALT rises above twice the upper limit of normal, weekly liver function tests are covered until the ALT returns to the normal range. Where elimination of teriflunomide is required, two serum
  • teriflunomide concentrations obtained at least 14 days apart are covered.
  • Azathioprine, a CBC and platelet count are covered every 1 to 2 weeks with any change of dose and every 1 to 3 months thereafter, with liver function tests every 3 months.
  • Azathioprine, TPMT and NUDT15 testing is covered before treatment only if one of the following applies:
  • A: The baseline absolute lymphocyte count is below 800/microL; or
  • B: The patient is taking allopurinol and there is no alternative to starting azathioprine.
  • Hydroxychloroquinen, annual ophthalmologic evaluation for retinal toxicity is covered only. no routine lab toxicity is covered.
  • Biologic DMARDs:
  • TNF inhibitor, a CBC is covered within one month of starting therapy and every 3 to 6 months thereafter while the white blood cell count remains stable.
  • Abatacept, no scheduled laboratory monitoring is covered.
  • IL-6 receptor inhibitor, a CBC with differential and liver function tests comprising ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are covered monthly for the first 3 months of therapy and every 3 months thereafter.
  • A lipid panel is covered 4 to 8 weeks after starting therapy and every 6 months thereafter.
  • Rituximab, a CBC with differential is covered 4 to 6 weeks after each treatment course, and at any time up to one year after an infusion where a severe infection or unusual severe mouth ulceration or mucositis
  • develops. Serum immunoglobulins are covered before each retreatment and where a serious or repeated infection develops.
  • Where a bDMARD is given together with a csDMARD, the monitoring schedule for that csDMARD continues in full and is covered in addition to the schedule above.
  • JAK Inhibitors:
  • The following are covered:
  • CBC with differential, serum creatinine and liver function tests comprising transaminases, albumin and bilirubin, monthly for the first 3 months of therapy and every 3 months thereafter.
  • A lipid panel 6 to 8 weeks after starting therapy and every 6 months thereafter.
  • Where a JAK inhibitor is given together with a csDMARD, the monitoring schedule for that csDMARD continues in full and is covered in addition to the schedule above.
  • Glucocorticoids:
  • For a patient on systemic glucocorticoid therapy, the following are covered:
  • Screening for glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes, at an increased frequency where the patient is on a moderate or high dose or on a prolonged course of low-dose therapy.
  • A fasting lipid panel.
  • Latent tuberculosis screening, where the patient is on high-dose therapy.
  • Non-laboratory. Bone mineral density measurement, where a prolonged course or a high dose is anticipated.
  • Non-laboratory. Periodic ophthalmologic examination, where the patient is on a prolonged course of moderate or high-dose therapy.
  • No scheduled CBC, serum creatinine or liver panel is covered for glucocorticoid therapy alone.

4. Documentation Requirements

  • Treating physician note stating the diagnosis of RA, the agent, the dose and the date of initiation.
  • For pre-treatment screening, confirmation that the agent has not previously been given and that the screening tests have not already been performed.
  • For on-treatment monitoring, the date of the last covered panel for that agent and any dose increase since that date.
  • For any concurrent csDMARD, the name of that agent and its dose.

1. Definition

  • Skin and soft tissue infection management centers on early recognition and standardized treatment of both purulent infections (furuncle, carbuncle, paronychia, abscess) and non-purulent infections (cellulitis,
  • erysipelas), with a primary focus on rapid source control, preventing escalation to deeper or systemic involvement, and guiding consistent, evidence-based care across ER and outpatient settings.

2. Scope

  • This guideline covers the diagnosis and management of skin and cutaneous infection, both Purulent & Non- Purulent.

3. Policy

  • Diagnosis:
  • o The diagnosis of skin infection is usually based on clinical diagnosis.
  • o Laboratory testing is not required for patients with uncomplicated infection in the absence of comorbidities or complications.
  • Blood tests (WBC, CRP): helpful in evaluating systemic response or monitoring progression in moderate to severe infections.
  • o Imaging:
  • Ultrasound may help to assess the presence of abscess and extent
  • Radiographic evaluation may be warranted in patients with underlying immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, venous insufficiency, or lymphedema and in patients with persistent systemic
  • symptoms.
  • CT scan: indicated if deep space infection, gas in soft tissues, or necrotizing fasciitis is suspected
  • Management:
  • Purulent skin and soft tissue infections:
  • Mild: without systemic signs of infection Moderate:
  • Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute, respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm3.
  • Patient with comorbidities Severe:
  • Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute, respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm.
  • Immunocompromise
  • Organ dysfunction (septic shock)
  • Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
  • Clinical signs of deeper infection
  • Infection that fails to improve with incision and drainage plus oral antibiotics.
  • Incision and drainage are indicated for all cases
  • o I&D for common cutaneous abscess should be done under Local anesthesia in emergency or outpatient setting.
  • o Situations where cutaneous abscess may require drainage under General anesthesia:
  • Pediatric age group.
  • Perirectal abscesses.
  • Anterior and lateral neck abscesses potentially arising from congenital cysts (eg, thyroglossal duct cysts, branchial cyst, cystic hygroma).
  • Abscesses adjacent to vital nerves or blood vessels (eg, facial nerve, carotid artery, femoral artery).
  • Breast abscesses, particularly those near the areola and nipple.
  • Large abscesses (>5 cm by palpation or ultrasound).
  • Recurrent and multiple interconnected abscesses.
  • Non-purulent Skin and Soft Tissue Infections (Necrotizing infection/Cellulitis/Erysipelas) Mild: without systemic signs of infection
  • Moderate:
  • Systemic signs of infection such as temperature higher than 38ºC, heart rate higher than 90 beats/minute, respiratory rate higher than 24 breaths/ minute, or WBC higher than 12 x 103 cells/mm3
  • Severe:
  • For patients whose cellulitis is associated with penetrating trauma, evidence of MRSA infection elsewhere, nasal colonization with MRSA, injection drug use, or SIRS

  • Uptodate - Skin Abscess Drainage
  • Daleel FM
  • British Journal of Anesthesia
  • CHI – Skin Infection
  • Saudi MoH - Skin and soft tissue Infection Management Protocol

Scope and test

Population: This uploaded decision guide applies to non-pregnant adults. For pregnant patients or children, it directs specialist consultation rather than applying this pathway.

Test: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]. This is a testing indication pathway, not a treatment or deficiency-threshold algorithm.

Source-derived clinical pathway (reconstructed from the original flowchart)

START — Is the patient a non-pregnant adult?
No: Consult a specialist.   Yes: Continue below.
↓
Is the patient symptomatic?
Yes: Check for proximal muscle weakness. Present → testing justified. Absent → testing not justified under this source pathway.
No: Assess age and risk factors below.
↓
Asymptomatic adult: age >65 years?
Yes: Testing justified under the uploaded pathway. No: Assess BMI.
↓
BMI >30?
Yes: Testing justified under the uploaded pathway. No: Check diet.
↓
Strict vegan, non-fish-eating or lactose-free diet?
Yes: Testing justified under the uploaded pathway. No: Check medications.
↓
Taking a medication listed in the source?
Yes: Testing justified. No: Check listed medical conditions.
↓
Any listed metabolic, gastrointestinal, hepatic or renal condition?
Yes: Testing justified. No: Check autoimmune conditions.
↓
Any listed autoimmune disease?
Yes: Testing justified. No: Testing not justified under the uploaded pathway.

Medications and conditions named in the source

Medications: anticonvulsants, rifampicin, cholestyramine, HIV/AIDS medication, antifungal medication, long-term glucocorticoid use.

GI and absorption: cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, post-bariatric surgery, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease), short-bowel syndrome, pancreatic insufficiency.

Other metabolic or organ conditions: liver failure/liver disease, chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism or hypoparathyroidism, hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia or hypophosphatemia.

Autoimmune diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus.

External guideline comparison — not identical to the uploaded coverage pathway

  • NICE PH56, recommendation 7: Avoid routine testing unless symptoms of deficiency, particularly high risk, or another clinical reason exist.
  • Saudi Choosing Wisely: Avoid routine testing in asymptomatic low-risk adults; consider testing for selected high-risk clinical conditions.
  • Interpretation caution: The uploaded flowchart uses age >65 years, BMI >30 and dietary categories as stand-alone positive branches. These are source-specific coverage rules and should not be represented as universally accepted indications for testing in every clinical guideline.
